## Two melodies, or one melody with filling underneath

Part 9 left you with a single line and a method for proving it matches its
source. Add a second line and the question changes shape. Two parts sounding at
once don't add up to *polyphony*, a texture where your ear follows each line as
a thing with its own direction. Give both parts identical attacks and identical
durations and they fuse. You'll hear one melody, thickened.

Disagreement is what pries them apart: different rhythm, different contour,
different register, different position in the phrase. Sonic Pi's concurrency
happens to fit that musical distinction exactly. A `live_loop` or an `in_thread`
lets each voice walk its own events at its own pace, `cue` announces a timing
boundary, and `sync` waits for one. Your voices can disagree inside the bar and
still meet on a shared grid, provided each process sleeps for exactly the
musical time its data claims.

Give every voice its own array. Tempo, meter and phrase boundaries are shared;
mutable note arrays are not. A loop that rotates or edits shared data changes
another voice between readings, and then you're debugging a concurrency fault
wearing a musical costume.

## A clock, a melody, and a bass

Below, one loop does nothing but announce the start of each four-beat bar. The
melody and the bass both wait for that announcement, then read arrays that share
no data at all. The melody makes four attacks; the bass makes three. Which of
the two do you expect to be easier to follow?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88

melody = [
  {note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :g4, start: 1.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: :a4, start: 1.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: :b4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
]

bass = [
  {note: :e2, start: 0.0, duration: 2.0},
  {note: :d2, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: :b1, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0}
]

define :play_events do |events, synth_name, amp|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.8, amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

live_loop :bar_clock do
  cue :bar
  sleep 4
end

live_loop :upper_voice do
  sync :bar
  play_events melody, :piano, 0.9
end

live_loop :lower_voice do
  sync :bar
  play_events bass, :fm, 0.55
end
```

This repeats until you stop it, so learn the shortcut before you run it: `Cmd-.`
on macOS, `Alt-.` elsewhere. Four or five bars is plenty.

Both parts leave the same known boundary at every cue. The melody climbs and
then parks on B for two beats. Underneath that held B, the bass moves twice more.
That's the moment the lower part stops being the bottom of a chord and starts
being a line, because it's doing something while the melody is doing nothing.

## Break the bar total on purpose

1. Shorten the last bass duration from `1.0` to `0.75`. The lower loop now
   reaches `sync` a quarter of a beat early and waits there. Listen to the hole
   that opens before the next downbeat. The clock stops the error accumulating,
   and it can't make a short bar sound complete.
2. Restore the duration, then give the bass the melody's four start times while
   keeping the bass pitches. Articulate together and the texture turns chordal.
   Compare that against the original, where the bass moved under a held note.
3. Add twelve to every melody note in the renderer. Timing hasn't moved at all,
   so anything you hear differently belongs to spacing. Wide registers make two
   lines easier to hold apart even when their rhythms agree.

## Why the cue survives sixteen bars

Each voice is a small state machine: find the next absolute start, sleep the
difference, play, advance the cursor, arrive at the shared boundary. Those
`:note`, `:start` and `:duration` keys are the same ones you built transcriptions
from in Part 9, which is the point. Arrangement doesn't get a new schema. The
clock holds coordination and no pitches, so swapping the melody array leaves the
bass and the clock untouched.

Sonic Pi counts musical time separately from the wall-clock time your Ruby
statements consume. Sixteen bars later, loops whose durations total correctly
still arrive at the cue together. A wrong total gives you a repeatable early
wait, a gap, or a boundary that gets missed entirely. So start every timing
diagnosis by adding the durations. No amount of balancing or synth-swapping
fixes a voice that claims the wrong amount of time.

`sync` also encodes musical form. Cue every bar when the parts renew every four
beats. Cue every phrase when the voices run unequal bars but share an eight- or
sixteen-beat arrival. Synchronise every note and you've coupled the lines so
tightly that separate processes buy you nothing. Pick the largest boundary that
holds your form together.

## Build eight bars that hold together

Write a two-part arrangement of eight bars and let it repeat for sixteen. Keep
upper and lower events in separate arrays, check every bar total, and choose one
cue per bar or per phrase. Give the lines attack patterns you can tell apart at
a glance, and start them at least an octave from each other.

Then mute each part in turn and listen to what's left. A line that survives on
its own has a contour; a line that sounds like scattered filling doesn't. The
combined loop should stay locked, and either score should be transposable or
replaceable without your touching the other one.
